title: 07. Advanced & Agentic RAG: What is JSON-RPC and Why MCP Uses It
summary: In the last lesson we learned that MCP is a standard "language" for AI agents and tools. Today we learn the exact grammar of that language — how messages are structured and sent.
objectives: ① Real-World Analogy — The Phone Order Analogy

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: **In the last lesson** we learned that MCP is a standard "language" for AI agents and tools. **Today** we learn the exact grammar of that language — how messages are structured and sent.

sections.title: ① Real-World Analogy — The Phone Order Analogy
sections.body:
Imagine you call a restaurant to order pizza. The conversation always follows the same structure:

```
YOU:      "Hello, I'd like to order a pizza" (you identify yourself)
THEM:     "What size?" (they ask for parameters)
YOU:      "Large, pepperoni" (you give parameters)
THEM:     "Order #4521 received. Ready in 30 minutes" (they confirm with an ID)
```

Now imagine calling a **different** restaurant. The conversation follows the **exact same pattern** — because that is just how phone orders work. There is an unspoken protocol.

JSON-RPC is that protocol for computers. It defines: **"This is exactly how you ask a computer to run a function, and this is exactly how it replies."**

sections.title: ② Plain English Explanation
sections.body:
**JSON** = JavaScript Object Notation. It is just a way to write data in a format that both humans and computers can read easily. You have probably seen it:

```json
{
  "name": "Veera",
  "age": 25,
  "likes": ["python", "AI", "coffee"]
}
```

**RPC** = Remote Procedure Call. "Remote" means on another computer (or another program). "Procedure" means function. "Call" means run it. So RPC = **"run a function that lives somewhere else."**

**JSON-RPC** = Use the JSON format to send those "run this function" messages. It is the combination of the two ideas.

sections.title: ③ Why Does This Matter?
sections.body:
MCP needs a way for the AI client to say "run the `read_file` tool on the server." It needs a standard format for this message so every client and server can understand each other.

JSON-RPC gives MCP that format. It is like the grammar rules of the MCP language.

Without JSON-RPC, every MCP server would invent its own message format — and the USB-C analogy would break down.

sections.title: ④ Step-by-Step Technical Explanation
sections.body:
### The Exact Shape of a JSON-RPC Request

Every JSON-RPC request has **exactly four fields**:

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method":  "tools/call",
  "params":  { "name": "add", "arguments": { "a": 5, "b": 3 } },
  "id":      1
}
```

Let us look at each field:

```
"jsonrpc": "2.0"
  → Always exactly this string
  → Tells the receiver: "I am speaking JSON-RPC version 2"
  → Like saying "I speak English" at the start of a call

"method": "tools/call"
  → The name of the function you want to run
  → MCP uses slashes: tools/call, tools/list, resources/read
  → Like telling the restaurant "I want to ORDER" (not "cancel" or "check status")

"params": { ... }
  → The arguments to pass to the function
  → Optional — some methods need no parameters
  → Like "large pepperoni" — the details of your request

"id": 1
  → A unique number YOU choose for this request
  → The server will use this same number in its reply
  → So you know which reply matches which request
  → Like the order number — "Order #4521"
```

### The Exact Shape of a JSON-RPC Response (Success)

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "result":  { "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "8" }] },
  "id":      1
}
```

```
"jsonrpc": "2.0"  → Same as always

"result": { ... } → The answer from the server
                  → Contains whatever the tool returned
                  → If result is present, there is NO "error" field

"id": 1           → SAME ID as the request
                  → This is how you match "reply #1 goes with request #1"
```

### The Exact Shape of a JSON-RPC Response (Error)

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "error":   { "code": -32601, "message": "Method not found" },
  "id":      1
}
```

```
"error": { ... }  → Something went wrong
  "code"          → A number that identifies the type of error
  "message"       → A human-readable description of the error
```

### Standard Error Codes You Will See

```
-32700  Parse error       → The JSON itself was broken/malformed
-32600  Invalid Request   → The request was missing required fields
-32601  Method not found  → You called a method that does not exist
-32602  Invalid params    → The parameters were wrong type or missing
-32603  Internal error    → Something crashed inside the server
```

### JSON-RPC Notifications — The Special Case

Sometimes you want to send a message **without expecting a reply**. These are called **notifications**. They look like a request but have **no `id` field**:

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method":  "notifications/progress",
  "params":  { "progress": 50, "total": 100 }
}
```

```
No "id" field → This is a notification
             → The receiver MUST NOT send a reply
             → Used for: progress updates, logging, one-way events
```

sections.title: ⑤ Beginner-Friendly Code Example
sections.body:
Let us simulate a JSON-RPC conversation in pure Python — no MCP library needed yet. This will make the concept very concrete before we use any libraries.

```python
# json_rpc_demo.py
# This is NOT real MCP code — it is a simulation to understand JSON-RPC
# We are just building the message shapes to understand what they look like

import json  # Python's built-in library for working with JSON

# ─── STEP 1: Build a JSON-RPC Request ────────────────────────────────

def make_request(method, params, request_id):
    """
    Build a JSON-RPC 2.0 request message.
    method     = the name of the function we want to call
    params     = the arguments to pass (as a Python dict)
    request_id = a unique number we choose to track this request
    """
    request = {
        "jsonrpc": "2.0",    # Always "2.0" — the protocol version
        "method": method,     # The function name we want to call
        "params": params,     # The arguments for that function
        "id": request_id      # Our tracking number
    }
    return request            # Return the dict so we can use it

# ─── STEP 2: Build a JSON-RPC Success Response ───────────────────────

def make_success_response(result, request_id):
    """
    Build a JSON-RPC 2.0 success response.
    result     = the actual answer (any Python dict or value)
    request_id = MUST be the same id as the original request
    """
    response = {
        "jsonrpc": "2.0",    # Always "2.0"
        "result": result,     # The answer from the server
        "id": request_id      # Same ID as the request — for matching
    }
    return response

# ─── STEP 3: Build a JSON-RPC Error Response ─────────────────────────

def make_error_response(code, message, request_id):
    """
    Build a JSON-RPC 2.0 error response.
    code       = error code number (e.g. -32601 means "method not found")
    message    = human-readable description of what went wrong
    request_id = same id as the request (even for errors, we match them)
    """
    response = {
        "jsonrpc": "2.0",           # Always "2.0"
        "error": {                   # Error object (never "result" AND "error" together)
            "code": code,            # Numeric error code
            "message": message       # Human-readable explanation
        },
        "id": request_id             # Same ID as the request
    }
    return response

# ─── STEP 4: Simulate a Full Conversation ────────────────────────────

print("=" * 55)
print("SIMULATING A JSON-RPC CONVERSATION")
print("=" * 55)

# The CLIENT sends this request to the SERVER
request = make_request(
    method="tools/call",                        # "Please call the 'add' tool"
    params={"name": "add", "arguments": {"a": 5, "b": 3}},  # "with these arguments"
    request_id=1                                # "this is request #1"
)

print("\n📤 CLIENT SENDS THIS TO SERVER:")
print(json.dumps(request, indent=2))  # json.dumps() turns dict into a JSON string
                                       # indent=2 makes it pretty (not one long line)

# The SERVER processes the request and sends back a response
# (In real MCP, the server runs your tool and calculates 5+3=8)
actual_result = 5 + 3  # This is what your tool would calculate

response = make_success_response(
    result={"content": [{"type": "text", "text": str(actual_result)}]},
    request_id=1    # SAME id as the request — client uses this to match them up
)

print("\n📥 SERVER SENDS THIS BACK TO CLIENT:")
print(json.dumps(response, indent=2))

# ─── STEP 5: Simulate an Error ────────────────────────────────────────

print("\n" + "=" * 55)
print("SIMULATING AN ERROR RESPONSE")
print("=" * 55)

bad_request = make_request(
    method="tools/call",
    params={"name": "divide", "arguments": {"a": 10, "b": 0}},  # dividing by zero!
    request_id=2                # This is request #2
)

print("\n📤 CLIENT SENDS THIS TO SERVER:")
print(json.dumps(bad_request, indent=2))

error_response = make_error_response(
    code=-32602,                            # -32602 = "invalid params"
    message="Cannot divide by zero",         # Human-readable explanation
    request_id=2                            # SAME id as the bad request
)

print("\n📥 SERVER SENDS THIS ERROR BACK:")
print(json.dumps(error_response, indent=2))

print("\n✅ Notice: the 'id' in the response ALWAYS matches the 'id' in the request!")
```

**Expected Output:**

```
=======================================================
SIMULATING A JSON-RPC CONVERSATION
=======================================================

📤 CLIENT SENDS THIS TO SERVER:
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "add",
    "arguments": {
      "a": 5,
      "b": 3
    }
  },
  "id": 1
}

📥 SERVER SENDS THIS BACK TO CLIENT:
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "result": {
    "content": [
      {
        "type": "text",
        "text": "8"
      }
    ]
  },
  "id": 1
}

=======================================================
SIMULATING AN ERROR RESPONSE
=======================================================

📤 CLIENT SENDS THIS TO SERVER:
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "divide",
    "arguments": {
      "a": 10,
      "b": 0
    }
  },
  "id": 2
}

📥 SERVER SENDS THIS ERROR BACK:
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "error": {
    "code": -32602,
    "message": "Cannot divide by zero"
  },
  "id": 2
}

✅ Notice: the 'id' in the response ALWAYS matches the 'id' in the request!
```

sections.title: ⑥ Common Beginner Mistakes
sections.body:
```
❌ Mistake 1: Forgetting "jsonrpc": "2.0" in the message
   Why it happens: It seems pointless — why do I need this?
   ✅ Fix: It is REQUIRED by the spec. Without it, the server rejects the message.
         Think of it as the "area code" — you need it every time.

❌ Mistake 2: Using different ids in request vs response
   Why it happens: The developer generates a new random id in the response
   ✅ Fix: The response id MUST be copied exactly from the request id.
         This is how the client matches replies to requests.

❌ Mistake 3: Having both "result" AND "error" in the same response
   Why it happens: Trying to send extra info with an error
   ✅ Fix: A response has EITHER "result" OR "error" — NEVER BOTH.
         This is a hard rule in JSON-RPC 2.0.

❌ Mistake 4: Sending a notification and then waiting for a reply
   Why it happens: Forgetting that no-id messages get no response
   ✅ Fix: If you send a message with no "id", you will NEVER get a reply.
         That is by design — notifications are fire-and-forget.

❌ Mistake 5: Using id: null when you DO want a response
   Why it happens: Developer uses null thinking it means "any id is fine"
   ✅ Fix: null id means "notification — no response please."
         Use a real number (1, 2, 3...) if you want a response.
```

sections.title: ⑦ Quick Recap — What Did We Just Learn?
sections.body:
- ✅ JSON-RPC = standard format for calling functions on another computer
- ✅ Every request has: `jsonrpc`, `method`, `params`, `id`
- ✅ Every response has: `jsonrpc`, `result` OR `error`, and the SAME `id`
- ✅ Notifications have no `id` and get no response — fire and forget
- ✅ MCP uses JSON-RPC so every client and server speaks the same grammar
